modern_classification.accepted_framework: Six monophyletic subfamilies: Cercidoideae, Detarioideae, Duparquetioideae, Dialioideae, Caesalpinioideae, Papilionoideae.
modern_classification.mimosoid_note: Traditional Mimosoideae is not treated as a separate subfamily in the modern six-subfamily system; it is the mimosoid clade nested within Caesalpinioideae.
local_tracker_subfamily_breadth: Papilionoideae — Amorpha, Baptisia, Dalea, Lupinus, Sophora
mimosoid-clade flower architecture represented strongly in Joey media by Senegalia and Vachellia even though those genera are not currently among the seven Family Study Index genera
modern_classification.learner_rule: Use papilionoid, caesalpinioid-like and mimosoid as visual flower architectures. Do not present them as the old three formal subfamilies.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Find the fruit first. A one-carpel superior ovary that matures into a legume/pod or a modified legume is the strongest family thread. Then inspect alternate stipulate leaves, pulvini, and flower architecture.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Usually alternate stipulate leaves, often compound and pulvinus-bearing + one superior carpel/one locule + fruit derived from that single carpel, most commonly a legume/pod.
authoritative_framework: Habit ranges from herbs to shrubs, trees, vines and lianas.
Stipules usually present, although sometimes small or early-deciduous and sometimes modified into spines.
Leaves usually alternate and may be simple, trifoliolate, pinnate, palmately compound or bipinnate.
Pulvini are common at petiole and/or leaflet bases and may drive leaf movement.
Flowers range from strongly bilateral pea flowers to weakly bilateral/irregular or radially symmetrical mimosoid flowers.
Ovary is superior and usually formed from one carpel, one locule.
Fruit is usually a legume, but may be indehiscent, winged, fleshy, coiled, lomentaceous or otherwise modified.
Seeds often have hard coats and little or no endosperm.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach Fabaceae as always having a pea flower.
Do not teach all legumes as dehiscent pods splitting cleanly into two valves.
Do not teach all leaves as pinnately compound; Cercis is simple-leaved and Lupinus is palmately compound.
Do not teach stipules as always obvious; they may be minute or caducous.
Do not use nitrogen-fixing nodules as a field ID test or uproot plants to look for them.
Do not teach Mimosoideae as a current formal subfamily.
Do not assume 10 stamens; number and fusion vary enormously across the family.

anatomy: stamens often 10 and commonly fused in various patterns
anchor_details: Palmately compound 5–6 leaflet leaves with stipules.
Five petals: banner, two wings, two fused keel petals.
Ten monadelphous stamens in the UT Williamson treatment.
Dehiscent multi-seeded legume whose valves separate and twist.

anatomy: Flowers bilateral to irregular but do not use the standard pea-flower overlap pattern.
Stamens often free or heteromorphic depending on genus.
Single superior carpel still ties the architecture back to Fabaceae.
anchor_details: Simple heart-shaped leaves are a major leaf exception.
Flowers arise in clustered racemes on older woody twigs/short shoots.
Five unequal free petals; keel petals are not fused.

flower_architecture_cards.role: family-breadth visual architecture; modern Caesalpinioideae, not a separate subfamily
anatomy: Flowers tiny and radial in heads or spikes.
The showy part is frequently many long exserted stamens rather than large petals.
Legume fruit remains the family anchor.

exception_cards.lesson: papilionoid lineage with most of the pea corolla missing
key_points: Corolla reduced to one standard/banner petal.
Wings and keel absent.
Ten stamens remain conspicuous.
Fruit is a small indehiscent legume, often one-seeded.
This prevents the learner from making 'banner + wings + keel' mandatory for Fabaceae.
Headlike spikes of small bilateral flowers.
Petal/stamen organization is highly specialized.
The fruit can be tiny, indehiscent and only one-seeded rather than a familiar bean pod.
UT Williamson Dalea treatments show the pod being shed within the persistent calyx.
Simple cordate leaves rather than compound leaves.
Flowers borne directly from woody twigs/short shoots.
Five unequal petals and ten free stamens.
Flattened legume makes family membership obvious after flowering.
Useful counterexample to the pea-flower pattern.
Yellow irregular flowers with unequal stamens/anthers in many Senna species.
Still resolves to one superior carpel and a legume fruit.

exception_cards.lesson: woody papilionoid legume with conspicuous seeds
key_points: Evergreen woody local form in S. secundiflora.
Pinnate leaves and pea-like flowers.
Woody necklace-like legume provides a strong fruit cue.
Red seeds are visually distinctive; do not use ingestion/taste as an ID test.

fruit_lesson.key_point: The legume is the safest structural thread through the family's extreme floral diversity.
sequence: pod opened to show seeds along one suture
compare modified fruits: Dalea one-seeded indehiscent pod, Cercis flattened pod, Lupinus dehiscent twisting pod, Amorpha tiny indehiscent pod

leaf_lesson.key_point: Compound leaves are common, but the family is too diverse for 'legume = pinnate leaf.'
comparison: stipules and pulvini remain useful supporting characters

Polygalaceae.confusion: Some milkworts have superficially pea-like bilateral flowers.
Polygalaceae.tie_breaker: Polygalaceae usually has simple exstipulate leaves and a highly modified sepal/petal flower, then a capsule rather than a one-carpel legume. Fabaceae typically has stipules/pulvini and the single-carpel pod framework.

Rosaceae.confusion: Both commonly have stipules and compound leaves.
Rosaceae.tie_breaker: Rosaceae commonly has a hypanthium and many free stamens/carpels or fused pome ovaries, with drupes/pomes/achenes. Fabaceae centers on one superior carpel producing a legume.

Bignoniaceae.confusion: Some woody plants have compound leaves and showy bilateral flowers.
Bignoniaceae.tie_breaker: Bignoniaceae generally has opposite leaves, a fused corolla and a 2-carpellate capsule. Fabaceae usually has alternate stipulate leaves, free petals in its showy bilateral forms and a one-carpel legume.
